analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum nurse-to-patient staffing ratios in hospitals and protects nurses who refuse unsafe assignments.
analysis.headline: The bill won the support of 88 House Democrats but was never voted on, dying in committee without a hearing or floor vote in the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every hospital in the country to keep a minimum number of registered nurses on each shift, with specific ratios set by unit — for example, no more than one patient per nurse in intensive care and four per nurse in medical-surgical units. Hospitals would have to post their actual staffing levels, keep records, and face federal fines for violations, and Medicare payments would be adjusted to cover the added cost. Nurses could legally refuse assignments that violate the ratios or that they are not trained for, without being fired, and patients could report understaffing through a federal hotline.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who would be cared for by nurses with fewer patients each, and registered nurses, who would work under capped patient loads, could not be forced into mandatory overtime to meet the ratios, and would gain legal protection for refusing assignments they consider unsafe. The bill also funds nursing scholarships, loan repayment stipends, and retention and mentorship grants.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets unit-by-unit maximum patient loads — one patient per nurse in trauma and operating rooms, two in intensive care and burn units, four in medical-surgical units, five in rehabilitation units [S3].

Hospitals could not impose mandatory overtime to meet the ratios, could not average staffing counts across shifts to appear in compliance, and could not substitute video monitors for a nurse at the bedside [S3].

Nurses could refuse assignments that violate the ratios or that they are not prepared for, and hospitals could not fire, retaliate against, or report them to licensing boards for doing so; nurses who prevail in court could win reinstatement, back pay, and attorneys' fees [S3].

Hospitals would have to post actual staffing levels in each unit and keep three years of records open to the public, and HHS could fine violating hospitals up to $25,000 for a first violation and $50,000 for repeat violations while publishing violators' names [S3].

The bill funds stipends in the nurse workforce loan repayment and scholarship program and expands nurse retention grants to preceptorship and mentorship projects, aimed at recruiting and keeping nurses [S2].

The bill's findings cite research including a 2014 Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality study concluding that increased nurse staffing improved quality and reduced length of stay at no additional cost, and a 2010 study crediting California's minimum ratios with improved patient outcomes and nurse retention [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would have to hire and orient enough registered nurses to meet the ratios and could face civil fines, though the bill directs Medicare to adjust payments to cover the additional cost of care for Medicare patients, and appropriates funds for federally operated hospitals [S3]. Taxpayers would absorb the Medicare payment increase, and in hospitals where hiring is difficult, units could face pressure if enough nurses cannot be found.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, and Medicare/taxpayers for the adjustment

drawbacks.text: Complying would require hiring many more registered nurses during a nationwide nursing shortage, and the bill itself directs the Secretary to report to Congress on ensuring enough nurses are available to meet the ratios — an acknowledgment that the workforce constraint is real [S3].
The Medicare payment adjustment means part of the compliance cost would be passed to taxpayers and Medicare beneficiaries rather than fully absorbed by hospital operating margins [S3].

Critics of mandated ratios argue that fixed numbers do not account for differences in patient condition or hospital design; the bill answers this in part by requiring ratios above the minimum based on patient acuity, but the floor requirements still apply to every unit, and the bill grants rural hospitals a longer phase-in (4 years rather than 2) in recognition of the staffing strain [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is straightforward: more nurses per patient means better monitoring and fewer medical errors, but also a large new hiring bill for hospitals, part of it shifted onto Medicare. The bill tries to soften both problems — Medicare payment adjustments cover the added cost, rural hospitals get four years to comply, and emergency exemptions exist for true crises, though the bill explicitly excludes understaffing itself from counting as an emergency. The serious risk is the nursing shortage: a ratio without enough nurses to fill it can push hospitals toward closing beds, which the bill addresses with recruitment and retention funding but cannot guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and then to a Health Subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on May 12, 2021, with 11 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committee on Ways and Means — a dual referral that means two committees would each have to act on it [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health; that was the last action of any kind, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed [S5].
The bill attracted 88 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no further action occurred through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals are better off because the bill died — no new staffing mandates, records requirements, or fines — while patients and nurses gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals that avoided the staffing mandate

sides.party_line_note: All 88 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republicans cosponsored, and the Democratic committee chairs who controlled the two committees of referral took no action.

industries.note: The bill would require hospitals to hire significantly more registered nurses, keep public staffing records, and face civil fines, with Medicare covering the added cost of care for its beneficiaries. The industry's interest in defeating the bill was to avoid those costs, which sit directly opposite the patient-safety benefit patients would have gained.

Nurses would work under capped patient loads, be barred from mandatory overtime to meet the ratios, and gain legal protection and a court cause of action for refusing unsafe assignments. Nursing unions backed federal ratio legislation.

The bill restricts hospitals from assigning temporary agency nurses to units without demonstrated competence and orientation, and bars counting video monitors or administrators toward ratios — raising the bar for cheaper substitutes for staff nurses, while the underlying shortage continues to drive demand for agency labor.
